findings.title: Index creation without CONCURRENTLY will lock writes on a production table
findings.explanation: A plain CREATE INDEX on Postgres takes a SHARE lock on `events`, blocking all INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE for the duration of the build. Events tables are typically large and write-heavy, so this can cause an outage or request pile-up. Use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS ...`. Note that CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block, so make sure the migration tool is configured to run this migration outside a transaction (e.g. a no-transaction directive), and handle the case of a failed build leaving an INVALID index (drop and retry).

findings.title: Missing IF NOT EXISTS / idempotency
findings.explanation: If the index was already created manually in production (common when someone has tried to fix a slow query by hand) or a migration is re-run after a partial failure, this will fail. Use `IF NOT EXISTS` to make the migration safe to re-run.

findings.title: No down/rollback migration
findings.explanation: There is no corresponding `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS events_project_id_idx;`. If the project's migration convention includes down migrations, add one so the change can be reverted cleanly if the index causes write amplification or planner regressions.

findings.title: Query/index match and benefit are not verified in the PR
findings.explanation: The PR claims the query does a sequential scan, but includes no EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before/after, and the query itself is not in the diff. Please confirm the endpoint filters by `project_id` and orders by `id DESC` (with keyset pagination on `id < ?` and a LIMIT) so the index is actually used and no extra sort is needed. If the query also filters on other columns (e.g. event type or created_at), a different or partial index may be better. Also check whether an existing index on `(project_id)` becomes redundant and can be dropped to reduce write overhead.

findings.title: Index name could be more descriptive
findings.explanation: `events_project_id_idx` does not reflect the column ordering. Something like `events_project_id_id_desc_idx` makes the purpose clearer and avoids confusion with a plain single-column index on `project_id`.

The project events endpoint does a sequential scan per project. Adds an index on `events (project_id, id DESC)` to match the query.

## Diff

```diff
diff --git a/migrations/005_events_project_idx.sql b/migrations/005_events_project_idx.sql

--- /dev/null

@@ -0,0 +1 @@
+CREATE INDEX events_project_id_idx ON events (project_id, id DESC);
```
